text: You're given an array called prices, where prices of i is the stock price on day i. Buy on one day and sell on a later day. Return the maximum profit, or zero if none is possible.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. So it's exactly one buy and one sell, and the buy must come strictly before the sell. For seven, one, five, three, six, four, the answer is five — buy at one on day one, sell at six on day four. And if prices only fall, like seven, six, four, three, one, I can't make a profit, so I return zero rather than a loss. Right?
Exactly. n is up to ten to the fifth, and each price is between zero and ten to the fourth.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would try every buy and sell pair. That's quadratic — about ten to the tenth steps, way too slow. The key insight is to fix the sell day. To maximize today's price minus the buy price, I just want the smallest price to the left of today. This problem reminds me of a running-minimum scan — really a sliding window whose left edge is pinned to the cheapest day so far. One left-to-right pass, keep the minimum, and at each day compute the sell-today profit against it. That's linear time and constant space.

Here's the plan. One: start with min price as the first price, and max profit as zero. Two: for each later day, first update max profit with today's price minus min price, using the old minimum. Three: then lower min price with today's price. One thing worth flagging — the order. Profit first means the buy is always on an earlier day. Swapping the two lines would only add a same-day trade worth zero, so the answer survives, but this order states the rule directly. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, here's the running-minimum version. One loop from day one: update the best profit, then lower the minimum. The easy line to get wrong is the start value — max profit must start at zero, not negative infinity, so a falling market returns zero instead of a loss. There's also an equivalent Kadane view. On the day-to-day difference array, the profit of holding a stretch telescopes to the sum of its daily changes. So max profit is the maximum subarray sum: extend the held stretch, or restart.

Let's trace seven, one, five, three, six, four on the min version — expected five. Day one drops the minimum to one; from then on every row is just today's price minus one. The row that matters is day four, price six: profit five, which becomes the new max. Day five only gives three, so it returns five. That matches. Corner cases: the falling case seven, six, four, three, one — every sell-today profit is negative, so max profit stays at its initial zero. A single day — the loop never runs, zero. All equal prices — zero.
Why not just return the max of prices minus the min of prices?

That ignores ordering. In seven, six, four, three, one, the min, one, comes after the max, seven, so you can't buy low then sell high — the real answer is zero, not six. Keeping min price as a running min of only the days to the left enforces buy before sell automatically.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — a single pass with two constant-time operations per day. Space is constant — two scalars, no prefix array needed. Oh, one more thing — the natural follow-ups. With unlimited transactions, the answer is the sum of every positive daily change. With at most two transactions, it's a small state machine — buy one, sell one, buy two, sell two — updated each day, still constant space. With at most k transactions, the same idea uses k pairs of states. All the same backbone: one pass, tracking running extremes.
Clean. Good reframing, correct ordering, and you connected it to Kadane and the k-transaction variants. That's a wrap.
